points.as: the New York City Department of Health
points.question: What do you do?

options.text: Announce an outbreak to the public at once.
Look for further cases and start active surveillance.
Ask the state's wildlife and veterinary services whether they have seen anything similar.
Wait for laboratory results on the two patients.

before.q: identified an initial cluster of six patients.
before.who: New York City Department of Health

before.q: Westchester and Nassau county health departments: began active surveillance on 3 September.

options.text: An outbreak of encephalitis whose cause is not yet confirmed.
Nothing yet: first ask the animal-health laboratories whether birds are dying too.
An outbreak of St. Louis encephalitis.
A possible deliberate release, pending further tests.

did_q.q: CDC announced it on 3 September as St. Louis encephalitis, a virus never before documented in the city.

then.q: The Bronx Zoo's head pathologist: obtained the agreement of the US Army Medical Research Institute of Infectious Diseases to try to identify the virus in birds.

before.q: bird tissues went to the USDA National Veterinary Services Laboratories on 10 September and virus isolates to CDC on 20 September.

points.question: What do you do with the virus isolated from the birds?

options.text: Hold to the St. Louis encephalitis finding; the bird deaths are a separate matter.
Sequence the isolates and set them beside the agent in the human cases.
Leave the bird isolates to the veterinary laboratories.

did_q.q: At CDC on 23 September polymerase chain reaction and DNA sequencing showed that the isolates were closely related to West Nile virus.
From 23 September an academic researcher at the University of California at Irvine and CDC came to the same conclusion that the agent was something else.

then.q: By the week of 27 September CDC had confirmed a West Nile-like virus.
As of 28 September the agencies recorded 17 confirmed and 20 probable human cases and four deaths.

before.q: an October 1999 media report suggested an unnatural origin

points.question: What do you do with the allegation?

options.text: Treat the outbreak as a possible attack and say so.
Leave it to the health agencies; a virus is not an intelligence matter.
Examine the allegation and report what you find.

did.q: the Central Intelligence Agency examined the allegations and concluded that there was no indication of intentional causation

then.q: Health officials confirmed 62 human cases, of whom 7 died.
